questions.question: What must be specified before something can be called an algebraic structure?
options: A list of equations but no underlying set
A vector space basis only
A single number together with no operation
A set and one or more operations on that set
questions.explanation: An algebraic structure requires a set together with one or more operations on that set.
questions.source_support: Definition: an algebraic structure consists of a set together with one or more operations on that set.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Identify the ingredients of an algebraic structure.
option_explanations: Equations without an underlying set are not a structure.
A vector-space basis alone is not the requirement.
A single number with no operation is not a structure.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: In an algebraic structure, what is the role of the set?
options: It is the proof that every operation is associative.
It is always the set of real numbers
It records only the possible answers of an equation
It gives the objects to which the operations are applied.
questions.explanation: The set provides the collection of objects to which the operations are applied; the operations determine how those objects combine.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: the set gives the objects.
questions.skill_detail: Interpret the set part of an algebraic structure.
option_explanations: The set is not a proof of associativity; associativity is a property of the operation ($\star$), not of the underlying set.
The set need not be the real numbers; it can be any set, e.g. $\{0,1\}$ or $\mathbb Z$, with suitable operations.
It is not just the answers of an equation; it is the full collection of objects on which the operations act.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Why is the operation part not optional in the phrase “algebraic structure”?
options: A set alone automatically has all group properties
The operation is another name for the largest element.
Operations determine how elements combine or transform.
The operation is needed only for finite sets
questions.explanation: The operations determine how the elements may be combined or transformed, so they are essential.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: operations determine how objects can be combined or transformed.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Explain why operations are part of the structure.
option_explanations: A set alone does not have group properties.
The operation is not the largest element.
Operations are needed for any set, not only finite ones.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: What kind of information distinguishes a group from a ring or a field?
options: The order in which the elements are written on a page
Whether the set is described in English or in symbols
The names chosen for the elements
The number and properties of the operations
questions.explanation: Groups, rings, and fields differ in the number and properties of their operations.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: the properties of the operations determine what kind of algebraic structure we have.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Connect operation properties with structure type.
option_explanations: An algebraic structure is a set paired with operations whose properties (associativity, identity, inverses, commutativity) determine its type; the physical order of elements on a page is presentation, not part of the data $(S,\cdot)$.

The structure is determined by the operations on the set and their axioms, so describing $\{0,1\}$ in English or in symbols yields the same potential structures; notation does not change which axioms hold.

Renaming elements is an isomorphism of the underlying set, so the names $0,1$ versus $\mathsf{a},\mathsf{b}$ do not alter the operations; what distinguishes a group from a ring or field is how many operations act and which axioms they satisfy.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: If a structure is written as $(\mathbb Z,+)$, what does the symbol $+$ specify?
options: The fact that $\mathbb Z$ has exactly one element
The largest integer in the set
The inverse of every integer
The operation being used on the set $\mathbb Z$
questions.explanation: In $(\mathbb Z,+)$, the symbol $+$ specifies the operation used on the set $\mathbb Z$.
questions.source_support: Examples include $(\mathbb Z,+)$ as an algebraic structure.
questions.skill_detail: Read structure notation.
option_explanations: $\mathbb Z$ has infinitely many elements, not one.
$+$ is not the largest integer.
$+$ is not the inverse of every integer.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which of the following is an algebraic structure in the sense of the definition?
options: $(\mathbb R,+,\cdot)$
The equation $x+1=0$ alone
The phrase “all possible answers”
The number $7$ alone
questions.explanation: $(\mathbb R,+,\cdot)$ pairs a set with operations, so it is an algebraic structure.
questions.source_support: Examples include $(\mathbb R,+,\cdot)$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Recognise an example of an algebraic structure.

A phrase is not a structure.
The number $7$ alone has no operation.

questions.question: A student writes down the set $\{0,1\}$ but gives no operation. What is missing before this becomes an algebraic structure?
options: A proof that $0=1$
A choice of a largest real number
A rule for combining elements of $\{0,1\}$.
A polynomial whose roots are $0$ and $1$.
questions.explanation: Without an operation, $\{0,1\}$ is just a set; it needs a rule for combining or transforming its elements.
questions.source_support: Definition: a set together with one or more operations.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Detect the missing operation.
option_explanations: A proof that $0=1$ is not needed (and false).

An algebraic structure is a set together with one or more operations on that set; a 'largest real number' concerns the order on $\mathbb{R}$ and supplies no binary operation $\oplus\colon\{0,1\}^2\to\{0,1\}$.
A polynomial with those roots is not the missing piece.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For the candidate structure $(\{0,1\},\oplus)$, what must $\oplus$ do to be an operation on the set?
options: It must make $0$ and $1$ equal
It must ignore the elements of $\{0,1\}$ completely
It must assign a real number larger than $1$ to each input
It must assign an element of $\{0,1\}$ to each ordered pair from $\{0,1\}$
questions.explanation: To be an operation on $\{0,1\}$, $\oplus$ must be a function $\{0,1\}\times\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$, assigning an element of $\{0,1\}$ to each ordered pair (closure).
questions.source_support: The concept depends on binary operations on a set.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Apply the operation-on-a-set idea.
option_explanations: It need not make $0$ and $1$ equal; they remain distinct elements, and the operation assigns an output in $\{0,1\}$ to each pair without identifying $0$ and $1$.

A binary operation on $\{0,1\}$ is a map $\oplus:\{0,1\}^2\to\{0,1\}$, so each input pair must produce a definite element of $\{0,1\}$; a rule that discards the inputs is not a function on $\{0,1\}^2$.
Outputs must stay in $\{0,1\}$, not exceed $1$; the codomain is $\{0,1\}$, so outputs larger than $1$ would violate closure.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which notation displays two operations on the same set?
options: $(A,B)$ where $A$ and $B$ are unrelated sets
$(+,\cdot)$ with no set
questions.explanation: $(A,+,\cdot)$ displays a set $A$ with two operations.
questions.source_support: A structure can have one or more operations on a set.
questions.skill_detail: Read notation for multiple operations.
option_explanations: $(A)$ shows no operation.
$(A,B)$ of unrelated sets shows no operation.
$(+,\cdot)$ has no underlying set.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: The integers with ordinary addition are usually written as which algebraic structure?
options: $\mathbb Z=+$
$(\mathbb Z,0,1)$ with no operation
$(\mathbb Z,+)$
$(+,\mathbb Z)$

questions.source_support: Examples include $(\mathbb Z,+)$.

option_explanations: $\mathbb Z=+$ is malformed.
$(\mathbb Z,0,1)$ lists elements but no operation.

questions.question: Why can the same set support different algebraic structures?
options: Every operation on a set has the same identity and inverses
A set can have only one possible operation
Changing the operation can change the algebraic properties
The set name determines all possible structures
questions.explanation: The same set can support different structures because changing the operation can change the algebraic properties.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: operation properties determine the algebraic structure.

questions.skill_detail: Explain dependence on operations.
option_explanations: Different operations need not share identity/inverses.
A set can carry many operations.
The set name does not fix the structure.

questions.question: Which property is most directly about how three elements are grouped under an operation?
options: Associativity
Polynomial degree
Existence of roots
Commutativity
questions.explanation: Associativity is precisely about how three elements are grouped under an operation ($(ab)c=a(bc)$).
questions.source_support: Relevant results mention associativity among properties determining the structure.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Link a property to operation behaviour.
option_explanations: Associativity states $(ab)c=a(bc)$, precisely a statement about grouping three elements; polynomial degree is the highest power of $x$ in $p(x)$, a property of a single polynomial rather than of grouping under an operation.

Root existence asks whether $p(x)=0$ has a solution in a field, a question about polynomials; grouping three elements under an operation is governed by associativity, $(ab)c=a(bc)$, not by solvability of equations.
Commutativity is about the order of two elements, not the grouping of three.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb R,+)$ not the same algebraic structure as $(\mathbb R,\cdot)$?
options: They use the same set but different operations
Only $(\mathbb R,\cdot)$ is allowed to use symbols
They have different underlying sets
Only $(\mathbb R,+)$ contains real numbers
questions.explanation: $(\mathbb R,+)$ and $(\mathbb R,\cdot)$ use the same set but different operations, so they are different structures.
questions.source_support: Definition: a structure consists of a set together with operations.

questions.skill_detail: Distinguish structures with the same set.
option_explanations: Both use symbols; that is not the distinction.
They share the underlying set $\mathbb R$.
Both contain real numbers.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Suppose $A=\{0,1\}$ and $a*b=a$ for all $a,b\in A$. Which statement correctly describes the candidate $(A,*)$?
options: It is not a structure because $A$ has only two elements
It is a field because every algebraic structure with two elements is a field
It is not a structure because the operation is not ordinary addition
It is an algebraic structure because the rule is an operation on $A$
questions.explanation: $(A,*)$ with $a*b=a$ is an algebraic structure because $*$ is a valid operation on $A$ (closed: $a*b=a\in A$).
questions.source_support: An algebraic structure requires a set and operations on that set.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Check whether a rule gives an algebraic structure.
option_explanations: Having two elements does not disqualify it; an algebraic structure can have any set, including $\{0,1\}$.
Not every two-element structure is a field; a field requires specific axioms (inverses, distributivity) that this left-projection operation lacks.
Operations need not be ordinary addition; any function $A\times A\to A$ (such as $a*b=a$) qualifies as an operation, regardless of whether it resembles addition.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

Listing the elements in a different order

Writing the same set as $\{\ldots,-1,0,1,\ldots\}$
questions.explanation: Replacing $+$ by ordinary multiplication changes the operation, hence the structure.
questions.source_support: The operations determine the kind of algebraic structure.

questions.skill_detail: Identify a structural change.
option_explanations: Reordering the listed elements does not change the structure.
Renaming a variable does not change the structure.
Rewriting the same set does not change the structure.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: A table gives outputs for $a*b$ for every pair $a,b$ in a finite set $A$, and every output lies in $A$. What has the table supplied?
options: A polynomial over $A$
A binary operation on $A$
A field structure with multiplicative inverses
A proof that $(A,*)$ is a group
questions.explanation: A table assigning to each pair $a,b\in A$ an output in $A$ supplies a binary operation on $A$.
questions.source_support: Definition requires operations; relevant results say properties determine the type.
questions.polish_notes: Removed internal key-result/example/page wording and strengthened visible distractors where targeted
questions.skill_detail: Separate operation data from stronger structure.
option_explanations: It is an operation, not a polynomial.
It does not by itself give inverses (a field).
It does not by itself prove the group axioms.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Why is closure usually checked before associativity, identity, or inverses for a proposed operation?
options: Associativity automatically implies closure
Inverses are meaningful only when the set is infinite
If outputs leave the set, the rule is not an operation on that set
Identity elements can be checked without knowing the output set
questions.explanation: If some outputs leave the set, the rule is not an operation on that set, so closure is checked first.
questions.source_support: An operation must be on the given set; operation properties then determine the structure.
questions.skill_detail: Reason about the order of structural checks.
option_explanations: Associativity does not imply closure.
Inverses are meaningful for finite sets too.
Identity elements need the output set to be well-defined first.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Before verifying any axioms, the notation $(A,+,\cdot)$ alone makes no guarantees. How should it be read?
options: As automatically a group under both operations.
A set $A$ with two operations whose properties need checking.
As a list of three unrelated symbols
As automatically a field
questions.explanation: $(A,+,\cdot)$ should be read as a set $A$ with two specified operations whose properties still need checking.
questions.source_support: Definition and relevant results distinguish the data from the properties.

option_explanations: It is not automatically a group under both.
The symbols are related (set + two operations), not unrelated.
It is not automatically a field.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Let $A=\mathbb R$ and define $a*b=a+b+1$. Which statement is correct about $(A,*)$ at the level of algebraic structure?
options: It is at least an algebraic structure because $*$ maps real pairs to real numbers
It fails to be a structure because $*$ is not written as $+$
It is not an algebraic structure because the formula contains $+1$
It is automatically a field because $A=\mathbb R$
questions.explanation: $a*b=a+b+1$ maps real pairs to reals ($*:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$), so $(\mathbb R,*)$ is at least an algebraic structure.
questions.source_support: A structure is a set with one or more operations on that set.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Check a nonstandard operation.
option_explanations: An operation need not be written as $+$; any function $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$, such as $a*b=a+b+1$, qualifies as an operation regardless of notation.
The $+1$ does not disqualify it; the output $a+b+1$ is still a real number, so $*$ is a valid operation $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$.

It is not automatically a field; a field requires specific operations (usually $+$ and $\cdot$) with inverses and distributivity, and the single operation $*$ does not by itself give $\mathbb R$ a field structure.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Let $A=\{0,1\}$ and define $a*b=a-b$ using ordinary integer subtraction. Why is $(A,*)$ not an algebraic structure with this operation on $A$?
options: Because subtraction can never be used in algebra
Because $0*1=-1$, which is not in $A$
Because $1*1=0$
Because the set has too few elements
questions.explanation: $0*1=0-1=-1\notin\{0,1\}$, so $*$ is not closed on $A$ and $(A,*)$ is not an algebraic structure with this operation.
questions.source_support: The operation must be on the specified set.
questions.skill_detail: Detect failure of closure for an operation.
option_explanations: Subtraction can be used; the issue is closure.
$1*1=0\in A$ is fine.
The number of elements is not the issue.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
